3.0.s.en: (1) What is the benefit of circumcision?

3.0.0.en: St. Paul begins this chapter with a question: if neither the Law nor circumcision justifies a person, why did God ask for it from the days of Abraham and Moses?

3.1.0.en: The Law and circumcision have many benefits, since God entrusted the Jews with His words and commandments, that they might keep them intact for all mankind. And in truth they were equal to the responsibility, but with formality and literalism in applying it.

3.2.0.en: St. Paul declares that man's unfaithfulness does not nullify the power and soundness of the commandment; the defect is not in the commandment but in man's inability to carry it out.

3.3.0.en: The word of God is always true, while man's objection and doubt is the lie, as was said in the Psalm (51:4). In His humility, God allows us to examine His words so as to discover their power and soundness. If man examines God's word in order to judge it, he will discover that God's word is righteous and true and overcomes all the arguments and words of men.

3.3.1.en: Do not hasten to murmur against God, because you are a limited creature and His wisdom is higher than your mind, and all His commandments are necessary for your life. Ask for His help and guidance, and you will understand and be able to apply His commandments; indeed, in proportion to your submission to His word, He reveals to you His wisdom in the ordering of your affairs.

3.4.0.en: Here St. Paul expresses astonishment and condemns the saying of people who toy with the idea that God's righteousness is displayed with sinners and fornicators: the harder the illness, the more the skill of the physician appears, and the more the iniquity increases, the more the competence of God appears in healing, sanctifying, and justifying. Then people say, "God who taketh vengeance" on us as a punishment for our sins "is unrighteous," because by our sins we displayed His righteousness, so He ought to reward us instead of punishing.

3.5.0.en: Here St. Paul condemned that idea by saying: how could God, the just Judge, be unrighteous?

3.6.0.en: St. Paul repeated the people's words in his own voice: "The more we lie and sin, the more the angels and the righteous glorify God for the greatness of His mercy and power." Then why am I still judged as a sinner when I am the cause of the glorifying of God?

3.7.0.en: Slanderously reported: that which we did not say is said in our name, and erroneous speech is attributed to us.

3.7.1.en: The Apostle Paul declares his distress at those who attributed to him a saying he did not say, namely: "Let us do evil" so that God will have mercy on us and give us good things, and so His holy name is glorified. It is as though Paul permitted the doing of iniquity. These in truth deserve judgment for this fallacy.

3.7.2.en: Beware, beloved, of this dangerous idea, for it calls for moral and spiritual laxity. God's mercy does not relieve the sinner of his full responsibility, by his will, for committing sin. So it is better for you to try from now to walk in the way of truth, to train yourself in doing good, so that people may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

3.8.s.en: (3) The sins of the Jews before Christ

3.8.0.en: So that Christians of Jewish origin may not boast and say, "We are better than Christians of Gentile origin," St. Paul replies, denying that, and reminds them that he has declared in (chapters 1 and 2) that Jews and Gentiles have all sinned.

3.9.0.en: "As it is written": All the coming verses from verse (10) to verse (19) are verses from the Old Testament describing the sins of the Jewish people, which St. Paul quotes here to prove by them that they were a people who greatly provoked God.

3.9.1.en: St. Paul began with the verse "there is none that doeth good, no, not one" (Ps 14:3). Even the saints in the Old Testament had their faults, and those of whom Scripture said that they were righteous, like Elizabeth and Zacharias, had an imperfect righteousness, because Christ had not yet accomplished redemption. Therefore, when the righteous died, they went to Hades even though they were righteous, and did not enter Paradise until after the crucifixion and death of Christ. Only then did they begin to enjoy complete justification.

3.10.0.en: This verse, from Ps (53:2), shows that the Jews preserved the verses and words of the Law, but did not understand the purpose behind them, and did not love God from their hearts, which is the goal of the Law.

3.11.0.en: Gone out of the way: they went far away and turned aside from the way of truth.

3.11.1.en: God shows in (Ps 14:3) that all have fallen into corruption, and not even one good person was found.

3.11.2.en: There are sins that are widespread and prevailing in the society around you; do not be swept into them because many have fallen into committing them.

3.12.1.en: God declares in (Ps 5:9) that the mouth of the wicked, which speaks plots and false testimonies, was the cause of the killing of many innocent people, and they are like serpents, speaking with cunning and hypocrisy, as if they were friends, but their tongue carries deadly danger.

3.12.2.en: Here ask yourself: is your tongue a cause of blessing for others, or a cause of harm and bitterness for them?

3.13.0.en: Here Paul cites the words of the Psalm (Ps 10:7), which shows how sinners curse everyone and murmur against everything.

3.13.1.en: Beware of murmuring, and do not think that God has singled you out for the greatest share of the world's calamities, but thank Him for the many good things He bestows upon you.

3.14.0.en: Isaiah shows in (Isa 59:7, 8) the swiftness of the wicked in killing others. They were not content with robbery, that is, stealing from others, but worked to crush and shatter them, like King Ahab, who killed Naboth the Jezreelite in order to seize his field. As a result of all these deeds, they lost their inner peace, "There is no peace, saith the Lord, unto the wicked" (Isa 48:22).

3.15.0.en: The Psalm (36:1) reveals the reason for these sins, which is that they did not set the fear of God before them when they were committing them.

3.16.1.en: It is obvious that what the Law said in the preceding verses is directed to those who are under the Law, that is, the Jews, so that every Jewish mouth may be stopped and they have no argument with which to defend themselves by their mouths. Thus the whole world in both its parts, Jews and Gentiles, becomes deserving of punishment and death from God.

3.17.0.en: Before Him: that is, before the Law, because the Law made us know the meaning of sin, as though it were a book of statutes and penalties that came to regulate the life of man, who had lived without a religion to restrain him or a law to deter him. So every person found himself unrighteous because he fell short in carrying out the commandments of the Law.

3.18.0.en: But now the righteousness of God, which was accomplished by redemption, has been manifested to us and we have seen it. It is the turning point in the spiritual history of mankind without the Law, so that salvation became possible without the need for the works of the Law such as circumcision and blood sacrifices. And this righteousness through the redemption of Christ is not a new idea to mankind; rather, all the prophets spoke of it, and all the ordinances of the Law, the rites, and the sacrifices pointed to it and prepared the way for it.

3.19.0.en: The righteousness of God by faith: that is, the salvation offered to mankind so that we may believe in it. Unto all: that is, every soul, whether Jew or Gentile; there is no difference with God.

3.20.0.en: All people were equal before God in regard to their sins, which caused man to lose his glory as one like God, in His image and likeness, so that man became in the utmost need and want of his lost glory.

3.21.0.en: Christ bore all our sins and died for us, and in this we are justified freely if we believe in His redemption.

3.22.0.en: This justification by the blood of Christ also works retroactively, to atone for our past sins, or the sins of those who died in the faith awaiting Christ the Savior.

3.23.0.en: God's plan from eternity is the justification and redemption of man, and this was accomplished by the crucifixion of Christ. God is righteous from eternity to eternity, but by His death He justified everyone who believes in Him.

3.24.0.en: The Jew must not boast of having accomplished the works of the Law, because they did not justify him; rather, he was justified by his faith in Christ.

3.25.0.en: God is certainly the God of the Jews and of the Gentiles.

3.26.0.en: The just God is one for all, justifying all by faith in Him, whether the circumcised Jew or the uncircumcised Gentile.

3.27.0.en: All this does not nullify or abolish the place and importance of the Law in the Old Testament, for it was a preparation for the salvation that Christ accomplished on the Cross, and our faith in Christ the Redeemer establishes the Law, which was necessary to prepare man so that he might know sin and reject it, and then Christ comes and removes it from him.

3.27.1.en: Believe in God's power that forgives your sins however many they are, and ask His help to free you from the hardest sins, and be confident that God rejoices in your repentance, your seeking of Him, and your striving to drive out sins and keep away from them. But on the other hand, do not depend on your intelligence and abilities alone to give up sins, but believe in God and ask for His support, and do all that is in your power, and you will receive forgiveness and peace.

4.0.s.en: (1) Abraham was justified by his faith

4.0.0.en: Hath found: obtained righteousness and salvation.

4.0.1.en: St. Paul asks what Abraham gained from his works according to the flesh, and whether he obtained righteousness by them? No, as he will answer in the following verses.

4.1.0.en: If Abraham's good works were what justified him, he would have the right to boast of them before people. But in truth he was not justified in God's sight by works, and when God justified him He did not mention that He justified him because of his works; rather, Scripture says that when Abraham believed God, only then did God count him righteous. And this is certainly grace, that God should count a person as righteous.

4.1.1.en: Abraham did not need the works of the Law, because it had not yet appeared. So he declares that the works of the Law are not needed for a person to be justified. This is, of course, different from the good works resulting from faith, in which we live now.

4.1.2.en: Our talk about Abraham's faith must not make us forget the importance of his works. St. James said in his epistle: "Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he had offered Isaac his son upon the altar? Seest thou how faith wrought with his works, and by works was faith made perfect?" (Jas 2:21-23).

4.2.0.en: Him that worketh: the works of the Law.

4.2.1.en: Grace: a free gift that gives salvation, justification, and entrance into the Kingdom.

4.2.2.en: Debt: God is in debt to give something in return for man's toil as his wages, which are material blessings on earth, but they do not forgive his sins nor does he enter the Kingdom.

4.2.3.en: St. Paul completes the answer to the question in verse (v. 1), saying that whoever deals with God only on the basis of his works according to the flesh receives his wages in material blessings, like a hired worker with his master, who owes him his wages in return for his works, and the matter ends without any additional grace or justification; that is, he remains a sinner who is not permitted to enter the Kingdom of Heaven. And here, beloved, are examples of this.

4.2.4.en: The Hindus, who perform very great ascetic works according to the flesh, are rewarded by God with wages according to their works, but they did not receive justification or salvation, since they have no faith.

4.2.5.en: The Pharisee, who did all the good works, boasting of himself, went out from before God unjustified, and even more, fallen into the sin of self-righteousness and pride.

4.2.6.en: So works alone do not justify, because before God they are nothing, for He says, "When ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do" (Lk 17:10), although works are necessary after faith.

4.3.0.en: Worketh not: the works of the Law, or works in which he relies on himself that have no relation to his faith in God, like the works of unbelievers.

4.3.1.en: Believeth: in Christ the Redeemer of all sinners.

4.3.2.en: The ungodly: the one who persists in evil.

4.3.3.en: Is counted for righteousness: his sins are forgiven, and he receives the righteousness of Christ and entrance into the Kingdom.

4.3.4.en: The ungodly who has sunk into the depths of evil and whom every way failed to change, if he is broken before God, confessing his faults without seeking excuses for himself, and declaring his complete readiness to change his ways and obey his Master, and to begin the straight and earnest path with God, confident of His power able to remove his sins, this person is counted righteous before God.

4.4.0.en: Without works: he had no opportunity to work, but died soon after his faith. Or what is meant is the works of the Law, which the Gentiles did not do, but when they believed in Christ they received justification. As David says, blessed is the man to whom righteousness is imputed without works. The phrase "without works" does not mean that works are unimportant, for their great importance was already pointed out in (ch. 2:6), but what is meant here is the one who was not given the opportunity for works, like the good thief, who did all that was possible of faith and witness to Christ in his circumstances, as a bound man hanging helpless on the cross, but his life was not extended further to do good works. He reached Paradise, and so did many others of the martyrs of pagan origin, who, when they saw the miracles and crowns of the Christian martyrs, believed and were even martyred in the name of Christ, dying before time allowed them to do good works. These received justification by faith and the baptism of blood without works.

4.5.0.en: The Psalm (32:1) bears witness to the happiness of those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered through God's mercies.

4.6.0.en: Blessed is he to whom God does not impute his sins (Ps 32:2), for He forgets them as though they had never been, while the criminal in the world continues to be pursued by his crimes, always written in his record, counted against him even after he receives his full punishment.

4.6.1.en: How great is the grace of God, which forgives our sins in the sacrament of confession, opens to us the doors of prayer and speaking with Him at all times, gives us His word in our hands in the Holy Bible, and cares for us in all our steps. Let us lift up our hearts in constant thanksgiving to Him, and meditate at all times on His many gifts.

4.7.0.en: St. Paul asks: does the preceding blessedness come upon the circumcision (the Jews) only, or upon the uncircumcision (the Gentiles) also? Of course it includes both.

4.8.0.en: Then St. Paul brings the decisive proof of the unimportance of circumcision in justification, by reminding the Jews of a historical fact of clear evidence, namely that Abraham was justified by faith while in uncircumcision, about 14 years before he was circumcised in the flesh, and before the written Law, which came by the hand of Moses more than 430 years after God's promise to Abraham.

4.9.0.en: Then after the justification, circumcision came as a sign of the justification and not a cause of it, so that Abraham might be the father of all those who walk in the same way of his faith and were not circumcised, that is, the Gentiles who believed in Christ.

4.10.0.en: Also that he might be the father of circumcision (the Jews), not of those circumcised in the flesh, but of those who walk in the same way of the faith of Abraham when he was a Gentile, that is, before he was circumcised.

4.10.1.en: Perhaps what concerns us in the above is that we should not rely on an outward form, or on superficial, showy worship, or on charitable works we have done, nor boast that we are children of the martyrs and saints, but we must have inner purity and a believing heart that loves God, ready at all times for good works as an offering of the love of God, and so God rejoices in us and counts us His sons.

4.11.s.en: (3) Faith is a condition for obtaining righteousness

4.11.0.en: St. Paul continues to prove his case by opening the door of salvation to all and not restricting it to the Jews by the Law, for the promise of salvation and the righteousness of faith was earlier than the Law and its works, because if salvation were restricted to the Law and its works, God's own promise would be nullified (God forbid) - "and in thy seed (that is, Christ) shall all the nations be blessed."

4.12.0.en: The Law came bringing with it penalties for the one who does not carry it out, and every person who knows the Law became condemned for transgression, that is, violation of the rulings of the Law. So how do we escape that transgression so as to obtain righteousness?

4.13.0.en: Thus God grants all mankind, who believe like the faith of Abraham, whether the Jews his children according to the flesh or the Gentiles, an equal opportunity to obtain the promise of righteousness, that is, God's pardon of our iniquities as a grace and a gift from Him, for we obtain righteousness not as a price in return for our faith, but as a great reward far beyond our deserts as human beings.

4.14.2.en: Scripture says plainly that God said to Abraham, "I have made thee a father of many nations," because God considers him a father of the Gentiles and the Jews.

4.14.3.en: Abraham's faith in God appeared in two situations:

4.14.4.en: 1- (God, who quickeneth the dead) When he obeyed God by offering Isaac his son as a sacrifice, he stretched out the knife to slay him, fully convinced that God would bring Isaac back to life again.

4.14.5.en: 2- (and calleth those things which be not as though they were) When he believed that he would have offspring (Isaac) even before he was born and existed.

4.14.6.en: Trust in the power of God, which is able to turn your weakness into strength, and if you fall into difficult sins He forgives you and turns you to holiness. Your faith will push you into positive action, not hindered by the multitude of your sins.

4.15.s.en: (4) All things are possible to him that believeth

4.15.0.en: Abraham, against hope and natural logic and human thought, believed in hope in God's power and ability to raise up the Gentiles from the darkness of sin and the shadow of death to become His sons, when it was said to him by God: "So shall thy seed be," O Abraham, many as the sand of the sea and the stars of heaven.

4.16.0.en: Abraham was strong in his faith, and gave no consideration or importance to the scientific fact that says a man cannot beget children when he has become old, and the deadness (death) of Sarah's womb (Sarah's womb), that is, the cessation of the ordinary course of women with her and her inability to bear children for a long time. He did not doubt for one moment God's promise, but believed it and gave glory and thanks even before the promise was fulfilled.

4.16.1.en: Beloved, you who desire to be a friend of God, do not be troubled if His promises are delayed, and do not doubt, for they are certainly coming at the proper time.

4.16.2.en: And do not let material calculations and human logic hinder your faith, for you are dealing with a God who is able to do all things, and what is impossible with men is possible with Him alone. So trust in Him and do not fear.

4.17.0.en: Here God rejoiced in Abraham's trust in Him, and counted him righteous in that situation also.

4.17.1.en: These words were not written to tell a story about Abraham that has ended, but behold, God's call is open to all mankind in general, and to you in particular. Let there be in you faith in the great, Almighty God, for He who raised up Jesus Christ from the dead is able to raise you from the death of sin.

4.17.2.en: Christ was delivered to death to die in our place because of our sins, and rose from the dead to raise us with Him from material, earthly life to a life of righteousness and spiritual conduct, that we may become righteous.

4.17.3.en: If the devil wars against you and you fall many times, do not be troubled, but believe in the risen Christ, and offer repentance that He may forgive your sins, and continue your spiritual striving; indeed, let your prayers and readings increase to make up for what you missed, and advance a new step in the way of the love of God.

4.17.4.en: The righteousness of Christ saves us from sin and gives us good fruits
